Everything between a trained model and a system that keeps working: the production lifecycle, registries and reproducibility, monitoring and retraining, the cloud and container platform underneath, the databases, caches and queues around the model, security and privacy, data validation, and the internal tooling that lets other engineers ship. It is the most widely named area in the sample: 87% of postings name something in it, and 61% ask for experience shipping ML to production end to end. It is tested in system design rounds, in the project deep dive ("how did you deploy it, how did you know it was still working") and in debugging scenarios.

## The senior bar

What separates a senior answer from a mid-level one in this area.

- Describes a model in production as a system with owners, SLOs, monitoring, a rollback path and a retraining policy, not as an artefact that was deployed once.
- Makes every model reproducible from versioned code, data snapshot, configuration and environment, and can say which of these a given past incident lacked.
- Monitors at four layers (service, data, prediction, outcome) and knows which signals are available before labels arrive.
- Chooses cloud services, storage engines and deployment strategies by workload and cost, with numbers, and knows where the bill comes from.
- Treats training data, model artefacts and credentials as attack surface and applies least privilege, isolation and auditability by default.
- Builds paved paths that other teams adopt voluntarily, and measures the platform by lead time and adoption instead of by features shipped.

### Shipping ML to production (end-to-end lifecycle) <span class="demand">61% of postings</span> {#production-ml}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.production-ml.0"> Walk through the lifecycle from problem framing to retirement and name the owner and artefact of each stage
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.production-ml.1"> Compare shadow, canary, A/B and blue-green releases for a model and say what each can and cannot detect
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.production-ml.2"> Decide between scheduled and triggered retraining and account for label delay and feedback loops
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.production-ml.3"> Triage an online metric drop into data, model, serving and measurement causes
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.production-ml.4"> Name the forms of hidden technical debt specific to ML systems

<details class="qa" id="mlops-001">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Walk me through the lifecycle of an ML system in production. What is different from shipping ordinary software?</summary>

The stages, each with an artefact that should exist when it is done:

1. **Framing**: the decision the model supports, the metric that defines success, a
   baseline and the cost of each error type.
2. **Data**: sources, labels, a versioned dataset and its validation checks.
3. **Training and evaluation**: reproducible runs, offline metrics on a fixed test set
   and on slices, a comparison with the current production model.
4. **Packaging**: the model plus its preprocessing, its input and output schema and its
   environment, registered with lineage.
5. **Release**: shadow or canary, then an online experiment against the business metric.
6. **Operation**: monitoring of service health, inputs, predictions and outcomes;
   on-call ownership; rollback.
7. **Maintenance**: retraining, re-evaluation as data shifts, cost control.
8. **Retirement**: migrating consumers and deleting data and artefacts.

What differs from ordinary software:

- Behaviour is determined by data as well as code, so both must be versioned and tested,
  and a change in either is a release.
- Correctness is statistical. Tests pass while quality degrades, so monitoring of
  outcomes replaces part of what unit tests do.
- The system decays without any deploy, because the world drifts away from the training
  data.
- Offline metrics are only a proxy; the release decision needs an online measurement.
- There are two pipelines to keep consistent, training and serving, and skew between
  them is a class of bug that ordinary services do not have.

In an interview, anchor the walk-through in one real system and say which stage was the
weakest and what you changed.

**Follow-ups**

- Which stage is most often skipped, and what does that cost later?
- Who owns the model after launch?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-002">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Compare shadow deployment, canary release, A/B testing and blue-green deployment for a new model version. What does each one tell you?</summary>

They answer different questions, and a careful release uses several in sequence.

| Strategy | How | Detects | Cannot tell you |
|-|-|-|-|
| Shadow | New model receives a copy of live traffic; its outputs are logged, not served | Crashes, latency, resource use, prediction differences against the current model | User impact, since users never see it; effects that depend on the model's own actions |
| Canary | A small share (1 to 5%) of real traffic is served by the new version, with automatic rollback on guardrails | Operational regressions and gross quality failures under real conditions, with small blast radius | Small effects on business metrics; it is sized for safety, not power |
| A/B test | Randomised split sized for statistical power, run for days or weeks | The causal effect on the business metric | Anything quickly |
| Blue-green | Two full environments; switch all traffic at once and keep the old one warm | Nothing by itself; it is a fast switch and a fast rollback | Quality differences |

A typical order: offline evaluation, shadow to validate serving behaviour and compare
predictions, canary with guardrail metrics, then an A/B test for the decision.

Model-specific points. Shadowing doubles inference cost and is impossible when the model's
output changes what happens next (an agent taking actions), unless side effects are
stubbed. Canary assignment should be sticky per user so that experiences are consistent
and so that state, such as caches and feature logging, is not mixed. Rollback must
restore the model, its preprocessing and its feature definitions together.

**Follow-ups**

- What are your automatic rollback criteria for a canary?
- The shadow model disagrees with production on 8% of requests. Is that good or bad?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-003">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span><span class="tag tag-rep" title="A third-party site lists a question on this topic as asked in an interview">asked at OpenAI</span> Three days after a launch that looked good offline and in the first day of the experiment, the online metric for the new model falls below control. How do you investigate?</summary>

Establish what changed before theorising about the model.

1. **Is the measurement right?** Check the experiment itself: sample-ratio mismatch,
   logging loss in one arm, a metric pipeline change, a novelty effect that was always
   going to fade. Compare day-by-day curves of both arms.
2. **Did the serving system change?** Deploys, configuration and feature-flag changes,
   dependency timeouts that trigger fallbacks, cache behaviour, latency. A model that
   times out more often silently serves defaults.
3. **Did the inputs change?** Per-feature null rates, ranges and distributions for the
   treatment arm against training data and against day one. Typical causes are an
   upstream job that failed or ran late so features went stale, a schema change, or a
   new client version sending a field differently.
4. **Is it a slice?** Break the metric down by platform, country, new versus returning
   users and traffic source. A drop confined to one slice points to data or a client
   release; a uniform drop points to the model or the serving path.
5. **Is the model feeding on itself?** If the model influences its own future inputs
   (recommendations, rankings), three days is about when feedback effects appear:
   reduced diversity, exhausted inventory, or features computed from its own outputs.
6. **Was offline evaluation misleading?** Leakage or a train-test split that did not
   respect time would produce a model that degrades as soon as it meets future data.

Mitigate first if the loss is material: roll back or reduce exposure, then diagnose on
logs. Close with the missing guardrail, such as a freshness alert or a slice monitor.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you distinguish a novelty effect from a real regression?
- Which of these checks can be automated as a pre-launch gate?

<div class="reported">

**Reported in interviews** (candidate reports on third-party sites, not verified)

- OpenAI, Software Engineer, Aug 2025: Diagnose a sudden accuracy drop in a deployed ML pipeline ([PracHub](https://prachub.com/interview-questions/debug-a-machine-learning-pipeline))

</div>

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-004">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> How often should a production model be retrained? Compare scheduled, triggered and continuous training.</summary>

Retrain as often as the world changes relative to what the model learned, and no more,
because each retrain is a release with risk and cost.

- **Scheduled** (daily, weekly, monthly). Simple and predictable. Choose the period from
  a backtest: train on data up to time $t$, evaluate on windows further and further
  ahead, and read how fast the metric decays. If a month-old model loses nothing, weekly
  retraining buys nothing.
- **Triggered.** Retrain when a monitor fires: input drift past a threshold, the outcome
  metric dropping, or enough new labelled data. Efficient, but depends on monitors that
  are neither noisy nor blind, and labels may arrive too late to trigger in time.
- **Continuous or online.** Incremental updates from a stream, used where freshness is
  the product (ads, feeds, fraud). Highest operational burden: any bad data flows into
  the model within minutes, so it needs strict input validation, automatic rollback and
  periodic full retrains to reset accumulated error.

Things that complicate the choice:

- **Label delay.** If outcomes arrive after 30 days, the newest month has incomplete
  labels. Train on matured data or model the delay explicitly.
- **Feedback loops.** The model's decisions shape its next training set; keep some
  exploration or holdout traffic.
- **Stability.** Frequent retrains can churn predictions for the same input. Measure
  prediction churn between versions and warm-start if it matters.
- **Gates.** Every automatic retrain needs the same evaluation gates as a manual
  release, compared against the current production model on the same fresh data.

For LLM-based systems the equivalent questions are when to refresh the retrieval index,
the prompts and the evaluation set, and when to re-qualify on a new model version.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you measure how quickly your model goes stale?
- What is the risk of retraining on data selected by the previous model?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-005">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> What is hidden technical debt in ML systems? Give the forms you have seen and how you contain them.</summary>

ML systems accumulate debt in places that ordinary code review does not see, because
behaviour depends on data and on other models. The main forms, following the well-known
Google paper on the topic:

- **Entanglement.** Changing anything changes everything: adding a feature or altering
  one input distribution shifts the weights of all others. No change is isolated, so
  every change needs a full evaluation.
- **Hidden feedback loops.** The model influences the data it is later trained on, or
  two systems influence each other through the world.
- **Undeclared consumers.** Other teams read your model's scores or logs without telling
  you; a recalibration then breaks their thresholds.
- **Unstable data dependencies.** Input signals owned by other teams change meaning over
  time; unused or weakly useful features stay in the model and remain a liability.
- **Pipeline jungles and glue code.** Data preparation grows by accretion into scrapes,
  joins and intermediate files that nobody can test end to end.
- **Configuration debt.** Thresholds, feature lists and learning settings spread across
  files with no validation or history.
- **Dead experimental paths.** Flags for abandoned experiments left in the serving code.

Containment: version and validate input data with contracts; register consumers and
expose a calibrated, versioned output; delete features that do not pay for themselves;
keep preprocessing in one library shared by training and serving; treat configuration
as code with review; and schedule the removal of experiment branches at launch time.
The useful interview move is to name one of these that caused a real incident and what
the fix was.

**Follow-ups**

- How do you find out who consumes your model's output?
- Which of these gets worse when models are replaced by calls to a language model?

</details>


### Cloud platforms (AWS, GCP, Azure) <span class="demand">37% of postings</span> {#cloud}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.cloud.0"> Map a training and serving system onto compute, storage, network, identity and managed services
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.cloud.1"> Apply least privilege with roles and service accounts and keep data on private networks
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.cloud.2"> Break a cloud bill into compute, storage, network egress and managed-service premiums and name the lever for each
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.cloud.3"> Decide between a managed ML platform and running your own on Kubernetes

<details class="qa" id="mlops-011">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Map a typical ML system, training plus online inference, onto cloud building blocks. What do you need from each?</summary>

Five groups of services, the same on AWS, GCP and Azure under different names.

- **Compute.** Virtual machines and GPU instances for training; an orchestrator for
  containers (managed Kubernetes, or a managed training and endpoint service) for jobs
  and serving; serverless functions for glue. Decide per workload between on-demand,
  reserved or committed capacity, and spot or preemptible capacity.
- **Storage.** Object storage (S3, GCS, Blob) for datasets, checkpoints and model
  artefacts: cheap, durable, high throughput, no in-place edits. Block storage and local
  NVMe for scratch and data caches. A warehouse or lakehouse for analytical tables. A
  low-latency key-value store for online features.
- **Network.** A virtual private network with private subnets, load balancers in front
  of serving, private endpoints to storage and managed services, and a gateway or CDN at
  the edge. Data location matters because cross-zone and cross-region transfer and
  egress are billed and slow.
- **Identity and secrets.** Roles for people and service accounts for workloads, scoped
  to the buckets and services each needs; a secrets manager and a key-management
  service; audit logs.
- **Managed ML and data services.** Training and endpoint platforms, model APIs, managed
  streaming, workflow orchestration, monitoring.

A training job then reads as: an orchestrated container on GPU nodes, with a service
account allowed to read one dataset prefix and write one checkpoint prefix, in the same
region as the data. Online inference: an autoscaled deployment behind a load balancer,
reading features from the online store, pulling the artefact from the registry bucket
at start, exporting metrics and logs.

**Follow-ups**

- Where does the first unexpected cost usually appear?
- What changes if the data may not leave one country?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-012">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> How do you set up identity, permissions and networking for ML workloads in the cloud so that a compromised notebook or job does limited damage?</summary>

Start from least privilege and from the assumption that any single workload can be
compromised, for instance through a malicious package or a poisoned model file.

**Identity.**

- Every workload runs as its own service account or role with a narrow policy: this
  training job may read this dataset prefix and write that checkpoint prefix. No shared
  "ML team" role with access to everything.
- Short-lived credentials issued by the platform (workload identity, instance roles),
  never long-lived keys in code, images or notebooks.
- People get access through groups, with elevated access granted temporarily and
  logged.
- Separate accounts or projects for development, staging and production, so that an
  experiment cannot touch production data or endpoints.

**Network.**

- Workloads in private subnets without public addresses; inbound traffic only through a
  load balancer or gateway.
- Private endpoints to object storage and managed services, so data does not cross the
  public internet.
- Egress control: training jobs and notebooks reach only an internal package mirror and
  approved hosts. Open egress is how data is exfiltrated.

**Data.**

- Encryption at rest with managed keys and in transit with TLS.
- Sensitive datasets in separate buckets with their own policies and access logs.

**Detection.** Audit logs on data access and permission changes, with alerts on unusual
volume or new principals.

The trade-off is friction: researchers want broad access and open internet. The answer is
a paved path, such as a sandbox project with de-identified data and a package mirror,
rather than exceptions.

**Follow-ups**

- A data scientist needs production data to debug a model. What do you offer?
- How do notebooks typically leak credentials?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-013">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Your team's cloud bill for ML has doubled. Where do you look, and which levers do you pull first?</summary>

First attribute the bill: by service, by team or project tag, and by workload type
(training, inference, storage, data transfer). Untagged spend is usually the first
finding.

**Compute, usually the largest part.**

- *Idle and oversized resources*: notebooks and development GPUs left running, endpoints
  with a minimum replica count sized for peak, GPU instances at 20% utilisation. Measure
  utilisation per instance; shut down on idle; right-size.
- *Pricing model*: steady baseline load on committed or reserved capacity; fault-tolerant
  training and batch inference on spot or preemptible instances, which are much cheaper
  but can be reclaimed, so they need checkpointing and retries; on-demand only for the
  remainder.
- *Efficiency*: batching, a smaller or quantised model, mixed precision, caching of
  repeated requests, moving offline work from online endpoints to batch jobs.

**Storage.** Checkpoints and intermediate datasets kept forever, many copies of the same
dataset, everything in the hot tier. Add lifecycle rules, retention for checkpoints
(keep the best and the last few) and colder tiers for archives.

**Network.** Egress and cross-region or cross-zone transfer: training in one region on
data in another, or chatty services across zones. Co-locate compute and data.

**Managed-service premiums.** Convenience pricing on managed endpoints, logging and
monitoring ingestion, and per-token model APIs. Check log volume and sampling.

Then make it stay fixed: budgets and alerts per team, cost per unit of work on a
dashboard (per training run, per thousand predictions), and quotas. Report the result as
unit cost, since total spend should grow with usage.

**Follow-ups**

- When is spot capacity a bad idea for training?
- How do you compute the cost per thousand predictions for a GPU endpoint?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-014">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Managed ML platform (SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML) or your own stack on Kubernetes? How do you decide?</summary>

Decide by team size, workload shape and how far your needs are from the platform's
defaults.

**Managed platform.** Training jobs, endpoints, pipelines, a registry and monitoring
without running the control plane. Strengths: fast start, security and compliance
features built in, autoscaling endpoints, little operations staff needed. Costs: a price
premium on compute, quotas and limited instance choice, opinions that are hard to bend
(custom schedulers, unusual serving patterns, multi-node training topologies), and
coupling of code to one provider's SDK.

**Own stack on Kubernetes** with open components for scheduling, serving, workflows and
tracking. Strengths: full control over scheduling and bin-packing of GPUs, any serving
runtime, portability across clouds and on-premises, lower unit cost at scale. Costs: a
platform team to build, upgrade and be on call for it; you own security patches, GPU
drivers and cluster upgrades.

Rules of thumb:

- A few engineers and standard workloads: managed, and spend the time on the product.
- Large or unusual GPU workloads, strict cost targets, multi-cloud or on-premises
  requirements, or dozens of teams needing shared quota and fair scheduling: own
  platform, when there are people to run it.
- Hybrids are common: managed Kubernetes and managed data services underneath, with your
  own job and serving layer on top; or model APIs for inference and your own stack for
  evaluation and data.

Keep the exit cheap either way: containers as the unit of work, artefacts in open
formats in your own bucket, and a thin internal interface in front of provider SDKs.

**Follow-ups**

- At what scale did, or would, the calculation flip for your team?
- What is the hardest thing to migrate off a managed platform?

</details>


### MLOps and ML CI/CD <span class="demand">34% of postings</span> {#mlops}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.mlops.0"> List what must be versioned to reproduce a model and how lineage links them
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.mlops.1"> Describe the stages of a model registry and the checks at each promotion
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.mlops.2"> Design monitoring that works before labels arrive, with alert thresholds that do not page on noise
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.mlops.3"> Compute a population stability index and explain its limits
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.mlops.4"> Design an automated retraining pipeline with gates and a safe promotion step

<details class="qa" id="mlops-006">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> What does a model registry do, and what exactly do you version so that a model can be reproduced and rolled back?</summary>

A registry is the source of truth for which model artefacts exist, where each came from
and which one is serving. For every version it stores the artefact and its metadata,
and it controls promotion between stages (for example candidate, staging, production,
archived) with a record of who or what approved each move.

To reproduce a model you need all of:

- **Code**: the commit of the training code and of the shared preprocessing library.
- **Data**: an immutable snapshot or a query pinned to a table version, including the
  label definition and the split.
- **Configuration**: hyperparameters, feature list, random seeds.
- **Environment**: container image digest, library versions, hardware type where it
  affects numerics.
- **Outputs**: metrics on the fixed evaluation sets, the evaluation set versions and the
  training logs.

Lineage links these: from a serving model you can reach the run, the data and the code,
and from a dataset you can list every model trained on it, which is what you need for
an incident or a deletion request.

What is deployed is more than weights: the preprocessing and postprocessing, the input
and output schema, thresholds and calibration, and for LLM systems the prompt, the tool
definitions and the pinned model identifier. Version them as one unit, because rolling
back the weights without the matching feature transformation is a common way to turn a
rollback into a second incident.

**Follow-ups**

- Two runs from the same commit and data give different metrics. What are the causes?
- How would you support "delete every model trained on this user's data"?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-007">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> You are asked to reproduce a model trained six months ago, and the retrained model scores noticeably worse. Where do you look?</summary>

Assume nothing was pinned until shown otherwise, and compare the two runs layer by layer.

1. **Data.** Most often the cause. Was the training set a snapshot or a query against a
   live table? Rows get backfilled, corrected, deleted for privacy or deduplicated
   differently. Compare row counts, label rates and feature distributions with whatever
   statistics the old run logged. Check that the split is the same: a random split with
   an unpinned seed or a changed user-to-split hash changes the test set itself.
2. **Labels and features.** Did a label definition or a feature's computation change
   upstream, so the same column name now means something else?
3. **Evaluation.** Is the metric computed by the same code on the same evaluation set?
   A changed tokenizer, threshold or metric library version moves numbers without any
   model change.
4. **Environment.** Library versions change defaults (initialisation, optimiser epsilon,
   data-loader ordering, mixed-precision behaviour). Use the old container image if it
   exists.
5. **Configuration.** Hyperparameters that lived in a notebook or an environment
   variable and never reached the tracked config; the number of training steps; early
   stopping on a different validation set.
6. **Nondeterminism.** Seeds, data order with multiple workers, nondeterministic GPU
   operations and distributed reduction order give run-to-run variance. Measure it with
   a few seeds: a gap inside that variance is not a reproduction failure.

Then fix the process: immutable dataset versions, image digests in the run record, and a
periodic "retrain from the registry record" job that proves reproduction still works.

**Follow-ups**

- How large a metric difference between seeds would you accept as noise?
- Bitwise reproducibility or statistical reproducibility, and why?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-008">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span><span class="tag tag-rep" title="A third-party site lists a question on this topic as asked in an interview">asked at Google</span> Design the monitoring for a model whose labels arrive weeks after the prediction. What do you alert on?</summary>

Monitor four layers, from the fastest and least specific signal to the slowest and most
meaningful.

1. **Service.** Latency percentiles, error and timeout rates, saturation, and the share
   of requests answered by a fallback or default. Alert as for any service.
2. **Inputs.** Per-feature null rate, range, cardinality and distribution against a
   training reference; freshness of every upstream table and feature; schema. These
   catch most real incidents (a broken pipeline) within minutes.
3. **Predictions.** Score distribution, the rate of each predicted class, the share above
   the decision threshold, and agreement with the previous model version on shadow
   traffic. A shift here with stable inputs suggests a serving or version problem.
4. **Outcomes.** Once labels mature: the metric itself, calibration and performance by
   slice. Until then use proxies that arrive sooner, such as user corrections, early
   partial labels, or a small human-labelled sample each day.

Alert design:

- Page only on signals that are actionable and specific: staleness, null-rate jumps,
  fallback rate, prediction-rate change beyond a band learned from history. Send drift
  statistics on individual features to a dashboard, since with hundreds of features
  some always look significant.
- Compare with the same hour last week to absorb seasonality.
- Monitor by slice; aggregate metrics hide a broken segment.
- Log inputs, model version and prediction for every request with a join key, so that
  outcomes can be attached later and any incident can be replayed.

The delayed labels also mean the newest training data is incomplete, which the
retraining pipeline must handle.

**Follow-ups**

- Which of these would have caught your last incident?
- How do you choose thresholds without paging on every holiday?

<div class="reported">

**Reported in interviews** (candidate reports on third-party sites, not verified)

- Google, Product Manager, Apr 2026: Metrics for the health of a production ML pipeline ([PracHub](https://prachub.com/interview-questions/measuring-the-health-of-a-production-ml-system-from-data-quality-to-business-impact))

</div>

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-009">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">coding</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Implement the population stability index for one numeric feature in NumPy. How do you read it, and what are its limits?</summary>

PSI compares the binned distribution of a feature in production (actual, $a_i$) with a
reference such as the training set (expected, $e_i$):

$$\mathrm{PSI} = \sum_i (a_i - e_i) \ln \frac{a_i}{e_i}.$$

It is a symmetrised KL divergence over bins, so it is non-negative and zero only when the
binned distributions match.

```python
import numpy as np

def psi(expected, actual, bins=10, eps=1e-6):
    """PSI of `actual` against the reference sample `expected`."""
    edges = np.quantile(expected, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf      # catch out-of-range values
    edges = np.unique(edges)                   # ties collapse bins
    e = np.histogram(expected, edges)[0] / len(expected)
    a = np.histogram(actual, edges)[0] / len(actual)
    e, a = np.clip(e, eps, None), np.clip(a, eps, None)
    return float(np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e)))
```

Reading it: the usual rule of thumb is below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 worth a look, above
0.25 a significant shift. These thresholds are convention, not theory.

Limits to state:

- Bins come from the reference only; quantile bins give equal expected mass, which keeps
  the estimate stable.
- It depends on the number of bins and on sample size. Small samples inflate it, so
  compare windows of similar size or calibrate the threshold by bootstrapping the
  reference against itself.
- Nulls need their own bin; dropping them hides the most common failure.
- It is univariate. It misses changes in the relationship between features and says
  nothing about whether the shift hurts the model. Weight alerts by feature importance
  and confirm with prediction and outcome metrics.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you compute it for a categorical feature with new categories?
- Why might you prefer a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, and when does that mislead?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-010">
<summary><span class="tag tag-staff">staff</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> Design an automated retraining pipeline that promotes models to production without a human in the loop. What makes that safe?</summary>

Automation is safe only if every judgement a careful engineer would make at release time
is encoded as a gate, and a failure of any gate leaves the current model serving.

**Pipeline.**

1. *Data build*: materialise an immutable training snapshot. Gate on data validation:
   schema, volume against expectation, null rates, label rate, freshness.
2. *Train*: pinned code, configuration and image. Gate on training health: loss within
   a band of previous runs, no NaN, expected duration.
3. *Evaluate*: the candidate and the current production model on the same fresh held-out
   window and on fixed regression sets and slices. Gate on no regression beyond noise
   overall and on protected slices, calibration within tolerance, and bounded prediction
   churn against production.
4. *Package and verify*: load the artefact in the serving image, replay recorded
   requests, compare outputs with the training-side predictions (skew test), check
   latency and memory.
5. *Release*: canary with automatic rollback on service and prediction guardrails, then
   full rollout. Register lineage and the gate results.

**What makes it safe.**

- The gates compare with the live model, not with fixed thresholds that go stale.
- A bounded rate of change: at most one promotion per period and a freeze switch.
- Rollback is one action and restores model and preprocessing together.
- The pipeline alerts when it has *not* produced a model for longer than expected, since
  silent failure means an ageing model.
- Periodic human review of gate statistics, and a holdout of traffic on an older model
  to detect slow degradation that step-to-step comparisons cannot see.

State where you would keep a human: changes to features, labels, architecture or the
gates themselves.

**Follow-ups**

- Each retrain is slightly worse than the last but passes the gate. How do you catch that?
- What is your prediction-churn metric and why does it matter to consumers?

</details>


### Containers and infrastructure as code <span class="demand">29% of postings</span> {#containers}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.containers.0"> Write an image for a GPU service that is small, reproducible and runs as non-root
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.containers.1"> Explain how the host driver, the container runtime and the CUDA libraries in the image must match
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.containers.2"> Describe the Kubernetes objects an ML service or training job uses and what requests, limits and probes do
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.containers.3"> Explain what infrastructure as code gives you, including state, plan and drift
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.containers.4"> Diagnose a container that works locally and fails in the cluster

<details class="qa" id="mlops-015">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">coding</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Write a Dockerfile for a GPU inference service in Python. What makes an ML image small, reproducible and safe, and how do CUDA versions fit in?</summary>

```dockerfile
# The tag is an example; pin the base by digest in practice.
ARG BASE=nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-cudnn-runtime-ubuntu22.04

FROM ${BASE} AS build
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends python3 python3-venv \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN python3 -m venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH=/opt/venv/bin:$PATH
COPY requirements.lock .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.lock

FROM ${BASE}
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends python3 \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* && useradd --create-home app
COPY --from=build /opt/venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH=/opt/venv/bin:$PATH PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app
COPY src/ ./src/
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "-m", "src.server"]
```

What to explain:

- **Layer order.** Dependencies before source code, so a code change rebuilds only the
  last layer.
- **Size.** A `runtime` base, not `devel`; no build tools or pip cache in the final
  stage. Framework wheels with bundled CUDA libraries are several gigabytes, and image
  size is pull time, which is cold-start time.
- **Reproducibility.** A lock file with hashes, a pinned base digest, no `latest`.
- **Safety.** Non-root user, no secrets in layers or build arguments, a `.dockerignore`.
- **Weights.** Usually not baked in: pull them at start from the registry, or mount a
  volume, so that image and model version independently. Bake them in only when
  cold-start time dominates.
- **CUDA.** The kernel driver lives on the host and is exposed by the NVIDIA container
  runtime; the image carries the user-space CUDA libraries. The host driver must be at
  least as new as the image's CUDA version requires. PyTorch wheels ship their own CUDA
  libraries, so the image's system CUDA matters mainly for other runtimes.

**Follow-ups**

- The image is 12 GB and pods take four minutes to start. What do you change?
- How do you pass a private package index credential at build time without leaking it?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-016">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Which Kubernetes objects does an ML inference service use, and what do resource requests, limits and probes do for a GPU workload?</summary>

The objects:

- **Pod**: one or more containers scheduled together on a node; the unit that gets a GPU.
- **Deployment**: keeps N replicas of a pod template running and performs rolling
  updates. A **Job** runs a pod to completion (training, batch inference); a
  **StatefulSet** gives stable identities and volumes.
- **Service**: a stable virtual address that load-balances across ready pods.
  **Ingress** or a gateway exposes it outside the cluster.
- **ConfigMap** and **Secret**: configuration and credentials injected at run time.
- **HorizontalPodAutoscaler**: changes the replica count from a metric.
- **Node pools** with labels and taints: GPU nodes are tainted so that only pods that
  tolerate the taint and request a GPU land on them.

**Requests and limits.** The scheduler places a pod by its requests. CPU above the limit
is throttled; memory above the limit gets the container killed (OOMKilled). GPUs are an
extended resource such as `nvidia.com/gpu: 1`, exposed by a device plugin. They are
integers and by default not shared: one pod gets the whole device unless time-slicing or
partitioning is configured. Set CPU and memory for the data-loading and tokenisation
work too, since a throttled CPU starves the GPU.

**Probes.**

- *Startup*: gives slow model loading time before other probes begin.
- *Readiness*: the pod receives traffic only when the model is loaded and warmed up.
  Without it, a rolling update sends requests to pods that are still loading weights.
- *Liveness*: restarts a hung process. Keep it cheap and separate from readiness, or a
  busy GPU causes restarts under load.

Also set a termination grace period and drain in-flight requests on SIGTERM.

**Follow-ups**

- What happens during a rolling update if readiness is missing and the model takes 90 seconds to load?
- How would you let two small models share one GPU?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-017">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> What does infrastructure as code give an ML team, and what are the failure modes of a tool like Terraform?</summary>

Infrastructure as code declares the desired resources (networks, clusters, node pools,
buckets, roles, endpoints) in version-controlled files, and a tool makes reality match.

What it gives:

- **Reproducibility.** A new environment or region is a parameter change, and staging can
  really mirror production.
- **Review and history.** Changes to permissions or cluster shape go through pull
  requests; you can see who changed what and revert it.
- **Disaster recovery and audit.** The definition of the infrastructure exists outside
  the cloud console.

How Terraform works, in one breath: providers map resource types to cloud APIs; a
**state** file records what the tool believes exists; `plan` diffs configuration against
state and reality; `apply` executes the diff; modules package reusable pieces.

Failure modes to know:

- **State.** It must live in a shared, locked, encrypted backend. Two concurrent applies
  or a lost state file are serious. State can contain secrets.
- **Drift.** Manual console changes diverge from the code; the next apply reverts them or
  fails. Detect drift with scheduled plans and remove console write access.
- **Destructive plans.** Renaming a resource or changing an immutable field becomes
  destroy-and-recreate, which for a database or bucket is data loss. Read the plan;
  protect stateful resources against deletion.
- **Blast radius.** One giant configuration means every change risks everything. Split by
  environment and by layer (network, cluster, applications).
- **Boundary with the cluster.** Terraform suits long-lived infrastructure; workloads
  inside Kubernetes are better managed by manifests or a GitOps controller.

For ML specifically: put GPU node pools, quotas and service accounts in code, since
these are what an incident or a new region needs first.

**Follow-ups**

- Someone resized a node pool in the console during an incident. What happens next?
- How do you keep secrets out of state and out of the repository?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-018">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> A training container runs fine on your workstation but in the cluster it is killed, hangs or runs several times slower. What are the usual causes?</summary>

Work through what differs between the two environments: resources, devices, storage and
network.

**Killed.**

- *OOMKilled*: the memory limit is lower than the workstation's RAM. Data-loader workers
  multiply memory, and page cache for memory-mapped data counts toward the limit on some
  configurations. Check the pod's last state and raise the limit or reduce workers.
- *Shared memory*: PyTorch workers pass tensors through `/dev/shm`, which defaults to
  64 MB in containers. The symptom is a bus error or a hang. Mount a memory-backed
  volume at `/dev/shm`.
- *Preemption or eviction*: spot nodes reclaimed, or ephemeral storage exhausted by
  checkpoints written to the container filesystem.

**Fails at start.**

- *CUDA mismatch*: host driver older than the image's CUDA libraries need, or no GPU
  requested so none is visible.
- *Permissions*: running as non-root with a read-only filesystem, or a service account
  without access to the bucket.

**Slow.**

- *CPU throttling*: a CPU limit of 2 with 16 data-loader workers. Libraries read the
  node's core count, not the container's limit, and oversubscribe threads. Set the
  worker and thread counts from the limit.
- *Storage*: reading many small files from network or object storage instead of local
  NVMe. Look at I/O wait; use sharded archives and a local cache.
- *Different hardware*: another GPU model, or a neighbour sharing the device or the
  node's memory bandwidth.
- *Network*: downloading the dataset or the model at every start.

Method: compare GPU utilisation, CPU throttling counters, I/O wait and memory between
the environments before changing the code.

**Follow-ups**

- How do you see whether a container is being CPU-throttled?
- Why does the process see 96 cores when its limit is 4, and what breaks because of it?

</details>


### Developer tooling and platform ergonomics <span class="demand">26% of postings</span> {#devex}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.devex.0"> Design a golden path from a new repository to a deployed model and say what is optional and what is enforced
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.devex.1"> Measure a platform by lead time, adoption and time to recover
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.devex.2"> Migrate teams to a platform without mandating it on day one

<details class="qa" id="mlops-029">
<summary><span class="tag tag-staff">staff</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Design the golden path of an internal ML platform, from a new idea to a model in production. What do you standardise and what do you leave open?</summary>

A golden path is the supported, pre-wired way to do the common thing. The aim is that the
easiest route is also the correct one, while unusual work remains possible.

**The path.**

1. *Start*: a project template creates a repository with the training entry point,
   configuration, tests, a container build, CI and a pipeline definition. First run in
   under an hour.
2. *Develop*: the same container locally and remotely; one command submits a job to the
   shared cluster; data access through a client that records which dataset version was
   read.
3. *Track*: runs are logged automatically with code version, data version, configuration
   and metrics. No extra code.
4. *Evaluate*: a standard report against the current production model and required
   slices.
5. *Register and deploy*: one command or a merge promotes a registered model to a
   serving template with autoscaling, logging, monitoring and a canary already wired.
6. *Operate*: dashboards and alerts exist by default; ownership and on-call are assigned
   at registration.

**Standardise** the interfaces and the things that are expensive to get wrong: artefact
and metadata formats, lineage, the deployment and rollback mechanism, security defaults,
monitoring, cost attribution.

**Leave open** the modelling: frameworks, architectures, training loops. Provide escape
hatches at each layer (bring your own container, your own serving code behind the
standard contract), so that the 10% of unusual projects do not have to leave the
platform entirely.

**Product discipline.** Treat teams as customers: interview them, build for the most
common painful workflow first, write documentation as part of the feature, keep
backwards compatibility, and publish what is and is not supported. A platform that is
mandated but worse than the home-grown scripts will be routed around.

**Follow-ups**

- Which part would you build first and why?
- A research team says the platform slows them down. How do you respond?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-030">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> How do you measure whether internal ML tooling or a platform is working?</summary>

Measure outcomes for the teams that use it, not the platform's own output.

**Flow metrics**, adapted from the DORA set to ML:

- *Lead time*: from a merged change, or a new training run, to a model serving
  production traffic. Also time from project start to first deployed model.
- *Deployment frequency*: model and pipeline releases per team per month.
- *Change failure rate*: share of model releases that are rolled back or cause an
  incident.
- *Time to restore*: how long a bad model or broken pipeline takes to detect and roll
  back.

**Adoption.** Share of production models on the platform; active users; and voluntary
adoption, which is the honest signal. Track the escape rate: projects that started on
the golden path and left it, with the reason.

**Friction.** Time to first successful run for a new engineer; queue wait time for
compute; CI and build duration; number of manual steps and handoffs in a release;
support tickets per user and their categories.

**Efficiency.** Cluster utilisation, cost per training run or per thousand predictions,
and idle resources.

**Qualitative.** A short regular survey and interviews. Ask what people did the last
time they shipped a model and where they waited.

Cautions: counts such as the number of pipelines or experiments are activity, not value,
and are easily inflated. Speed metrics must be read together with failure metrics, or
teams ship faster by skipping gates. And attribute carefully: compare the same team
before and after, or teams on and off the platform, while acknowledging that early
adopters differ.

The summary for leadership is one sentence per quarter: how long it takes a team to go
from idea to a monitored production model, and how that changed.

**Follow-ups**

- Which single metric would you report if you could pick only one?
- How would the metrics differ for a platform serving LLM application teams?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-031">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">behavioural</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Tell me about a time you had to get other teams to adopt a tool, platform or standard you built. What did you do when they resisted?</summary>

**What the interviewer is testing.** Whether you can create leverage beyond your own
code: understanding other teams' incentives, earning adoption instead of demanding it,
and staying with the work through migration, which is the unglamorous part.

**Structure of a strong answer.**

1. *The problem in their terms*: what the teams were losing without the standard
   (incidents, weeks per launch, duplicated work), with a number.
2. *Discovery*: whom you talked to and what you learned about why the existing way
   persisted. Resistance usually has a real reason: migration cost, a missing feature,
   a deadline, or loss of control.
3. *Design for adoption*: a first version aimed at one team's concrete pain, a migration
   path that is incremental, compatibility with what they already run, documentation
   and a working example.
4. *The first adopters*: how you picked a team that would benefit and be vocal, did part
   of the migration work for them and published their result.
5. *Handling resistance*: what you changed in response to valid objections, what you
   declined, and when you escalated or accepted that a team would not migrate.
6. *Outcome*: adoption, the metric that moved, and what you would do differently.

**Mistakes that sink the answer.**

- Presenting a mandate from leadership as the adoption strategy.
- Describing the teams as wrong or slow, with no account of their reasons.
- No measured outcome, or an outcome measured in features shipped.
- Stopping the story at launch, with the old system still running in parallel.

Use a real example and be specific about one objection you had not anticipated.

**Follow-ups**

- What did you do for the team that had a legitimate reason not to migrate?
- How did you decide when to deprecate the old way?

</details>


### Security, privacy and compliance in ML systems <span class="demand">21% of postings</span> {#security-privacy}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.security-privacy.0"> Give a threat model for an ML system covering data, model artefacts, the serving path and the supply chain
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.security-privacy.1"> Handle personal data across training sets, logs and derived artefacts, including deletion requests
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.security-privacy.2"> Explain differential privacy and federated learning at the level of what each guarantees and costs
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.security-privacy.3"> Design tenant isolation and audit logging for an ML product sold to enterprises

<details class="qa" id="mlops-022">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Give me a threat model for an ML system. What can an attacker do that they could not do to an ordinary web service?</summary>

Everything that applies to a web service applies here (authentication, injection,
secrets, dependencies). The ML-specific surface is the data, the model artefact and the
model's behaviour.

**Training time.**

- *Data poisoning*: an attacker who can influence training data, such as user-submitted
  content, scraped pages or a feedback signal, inserts examples that degrade the model
  or plant a backdoor triggered by a specific pattern.
- *Supply chain*: pretrained weights, datasets and packages from public hubs. Pickle-based
  model files execute arbitrary code when loaded. Prefer weight-only formats such as
  safetensors, verify hashes, scan and pin dependencies, and load untrusted artefacts in
  a sandbox.

**Inference time.**

- *Evasion*: inputs crafted to be misclassified, which matters most for fraud, abuse and
  malware detection where the adversary adapts.
- *Extraction*: repeated queries to copy the model's behaviour or recover its decision
  boundary. Rate limits and monitoring raise the cost.
- *Privacy attacks*: membership inference (was this record in the training set?) and
  training-data extraction, to which models that memorise are vulnerable.
- *Prompt injection and unsafe tool use* for LLM systems.
- *Resource abuse*: expensive inputs as denial of service, or stolen API keys used for
  free inference.

**Infrastructure.** Over-broad access to training data, credentials in notebooks,
unauthenticated internal endpoints, and prompt or request logs that contain sensitive
data.

Mitigation follows from asking, for each asset (data, weights, predictions), who can
read or influence it and what the worst outcome is. Then apply least privilege,
provenance and validation for data and artefacts, rate limiting and abuse monitoring at
the endpoint, and a response plan that includes retraining from clean data.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you detect that a feedback signal is being manipulated?
- Why is loading a pickle file from a model hub dangerous, concretely?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-023">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span><span class="tag tag-rep" title="A third-party site lists a question on this topic as asked in an interview">asked at Anthropic</span> Your training data and request logs contain personal data. How do you handle it, and what happens when a user asks for their data to be deleted?</summary>

**Minimise first.** Collect and keep only the fields the model needs. Drop or coarsen the
rest at ingestion (precise location to region, birth date to age band). Data that was
never stored needs no protection.

**Separate identity from content.** Replace direct identifiers with pseudonymous keys
and keep the mapping in a separate, tightly controlled store. Pseudonymised data is
still personal data, since it can often be re-identified by joining, but the separation
limits who can do so.

**Scrub free text.** Logs, prompts and transcripts contain names, emails and account
numbers. Run detection and redaction before the text reaches analytics or training
stores, and measure the detector's recall on a labelled sample, because it is not
perfect.

**Control and record access.** Role-based access to raw data, de-identified views for
most work, access logs, and encryption. Set retention periods per dataset and enforce
them with lifecycle rules, not by convention.

**Deletion requests.** Deleting the source row is the easy part. You need lineage to
find the derived copies: feature tables, training snapshots, caches, embeddings in a
vector index, evaluation sets, backups. Practical design: key everything by the
pseudonymous id, run a periodic deletion job across all registered stores, and rebuild
derived datasets from sources on a schedule so that deletions propagate.

**Models.** A trained model may have memorised the record. The dependable remedy is
retraining without it at the next scheduled cycle; machine unlearning methods exist but
are not yet something to rely on for guarantees. How regulators treat already-trained
models is not settled everywhere, so this is a decision to take with legal counsel, and
the engineering job is to make retraining and lineage cheap.

Purpose limitation also applies: data collected to provide a service is not automatically
usable for training. Record the permitted purposes with the dataset.

**Follow-ups**

- How do you find every place a user's data has been copied to?
- What would you log from an LLM product's requests, and for how long?

<details class="qa" id="mlops-024">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Explain differential privacy and federated learning. What does each guarantee, and what does it cost?</summary>

**Differential privacy** is a property of an algorithm. A randomised mechanism $M$ is
$(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differentially private if for any two datasets $D, D'$ differing
in one record and any set of outputs $S$:

$$\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon} \Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta.$$

The output barely depends on any one individual, whatever the attacker already knows.
Smaller $\varepsilon$ is stronger. Guarantees compose: every release from the same data
spends budget.

For model training the standard method is **DP-SGD**: compute per-example gradients, clip
each to norm $C$, sum, add Gaussian noise with standard deviation $\sigma C$, and step. A
privacy accountant converts the noise level, sampling rate and number of steps into
$(\varepsilon, \delta)$. Costs: lower accuracy, most painful for small datasets and rare
subgroups; per-example gradients are slower and use more memory; large batches are
needed; and the reported $\varepsilon$ is only meaningful if the unit of privacy (record
or user) is chosen correctly.

**Federated learning** is a system architecture. Data stays on devices or in silos; each
client computes an update on local data, and a server aggregates the updates (FedAvg
averages client weights after several local steps). It reduces central collection of
raw data. It is not a privacy guarantee by itself: updates can leak training examples.
It is combined with **secure aggregation**, so the server sees only the sum, and with
differential privacy on the aggregate.

Costs of federation: clients have different data distributions, which slows or biases
convergence; devices are unreliable and heterogeneous; debugging without seeing the data
is hard; and communication is the bottleneck.

One sentence to remember: differential privacy limits what the *output* reveals;
federated learning limits where the *input* travels.

**Follow-ups**

- Why is clipping per example, and not per batch, necessary for the guarantee?
- What does an epsilon of 8 mean in practice, and how would you explain it to a product manager?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-025">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> You sell an LLM-based product to enterprises. Design tenant isolation and the controls a security review will ask for.</summary>

A security questionnaire asks, in effect: can another customer see our data, can your
staff, where does it go, and can you prove it.

**Tenant isolation.**

- Every request carries a tenant identity established at authentication, and every data
  access is filtered by it in the data layer, not in the prompt. Row-level security or
  separate schemas, indexes or databases per tenant, chosen by the isolation a customer
  tier requires.
- Retrieval indexes are per tenant, or filtered by tenant and document permissions at
  query time, before the model sees anything.
- Caches, conversation memory and logs are keyed by tenant. A shared response cache
  without the tenant in the key is a classic leak.
- No training or fine-tuning of shared models on a tenant's data unless the contract
  allows it; per-tenant adapters stay per tenant.

**Data flow.** Document which sub-processors receive data (model providers, vector
stores, monitoring), with data-processing agreements and retention settings. Offer
regional processing when data residency is required.

**Access by your own staff.** Production data is inaccessible by default; break-glass
access is time-limited, approved and logged. Debugging uses redacted traces.

**Standard controls.** Single sign-on and role-based access for customer users,
encryption at rest and in transit, customer-visible audit logs of who asked what and
which documents were retrieved, configurable retention and deletion, secrets management,
dependency and vulnerability scanning, and an incident response process. Certifications
such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001 are evidence that these operate.

**Model-specific.** Treat retrieved documents and tool outputs as untrusted input, limit
what tools can do on a user's behalf to that user's own permissions, and test for
cross-tenant leakage as part of the evaluation suite.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you test that tenant A can never retrieve tenant B's documents?
- A customer asks that their prompts never be stored. What breaks, and what do you offer?

</details>


### Databases, caches and queues <span class="demand">20% of postings</span> {#databases}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.databases.0"> Match relational, key-value, document, columnar, vector and object stores to the parts of an ML system
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.databases.1"> Design a cache for model outputs with a key that includes everything the output depends on
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.databases.2"> Explain delivery semantics for queues and why consumers must be idempotent

<details class="qa" id="mlops-019">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Which kind of data store would you use for each part of an ML product: application state, online features, event logs, analytics, embeddings and model artefacts?</summary>

Choose by access pattern (point lookup, range scan, aggregate, similarity), latency, write
rate and consistency needs.

| Need | Store | Why |
|-|-|-|
| Application state: users, sessions, conversations, permissions | Relational (Postgres, MySQL) | Transactions, constraints, joins, flexible queries. The default until proven insufficient |
| Online features and session state at millisecond latency | Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB, Bigtable) | Point reads by key at very high rates, TTLs, simple scaling |
| Semi-structured records whose shape varies | Document store, or a JSON column in a relational database | Schema flexibility; weaker joins and constraints |
| Event streams: impressions, requests, tool calls | Log or stream (Kafka, Kinesis), landed in object storage | Append-only, ordered, replayable, decouples producers from consumers |
| Analytics and training sets | Columnar warehouse or lakehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, Parquet tables) | Scans and aggregates over billions of rows; poor at point updates |
| Embeddings | A vector index: an extension of the relational store up to millions of vectors, a dedicated engine beyond that | Approximate nearest-neighbour search with filters |
| Model artefacts, datasets, checkpoints | Object storage | Cheap, durable, large blobs; metadata in a relational registry |
| Metrics | Time-series database | Compression and rollups over time |

Principles a senior answer adds:

- Start with one relational database plus object storage; add a specialised store when a
  measured access pattern demands it. Every extra store is another consistency boundary
  and another thing to operate.
- Keep one source of truth per fact and derive the rest (caches, indexes, feature
  tables) so that they can be rebuilt.
- Online and offline copies of the same data will diverge unless one pipeline writes
  both.

**Follow-ups**

- When does a vector extension in your relational database stop being enough?
- Where would you store conversation history for a chat product, and why?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-020">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Design a cache for model predictions or LLM responses. What goes in the key, how do you invalidate, and when is caching the wrong answer?</summary>

**Key.** Everything the output depends on, and nothing else: a hash of the normalised
input, the model and preprocessing version, the prompt or feature-set version, decoding
parameters, and any per-user or per-tenant context that changes the answer. Omitting the
version serves old outputs after a deploy; omitting the tenant leaks one customer's
answer to another.

**Value and policy.** Store the output with its creation time and version. Set a TTL from
how fast the underlying facts change. Bound the size with LRU or LFU eviction.

**Invalidation.**

- Version in the key makes a model or prompt change an automatic miss, with no purge.
- Event-driven deletes when a source document or feature changes.
- TTL as the backstop.

**Operational hazards.**

- *Stampede*: a popular key expires and many requests recompute it at once. Use
  single-flight (one computation per key, others wait), stale-while-revalidate, and
  jittered TTLs.
- *Cold start after deploy*: a version bump empties the cache exactly when the new
  version is under most scrutiny. Pre-warm the top keys.
- *Negative caching*: cache failures briefly, or an outage is amplified by retries.

**Variants.** Exact-match caching works when inputs repeat (popular queries, item
embeddings, classification of repeated content). Semantic caching returns a stored answer
for a similar query by embedding distance; it raises the hit rate and can return a wrong
answer for a query that differs in one important word, so it needs a strict threshold
and an evaluation. Precomputation is a cache filled ahead of time by a batch job.

**When not to cache.** Personalised or fast-changing outputs, sampled generations where
variety is intended, low repetition (measure the hit rate first), and sensitive outputs
that should not be stored.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you estimate the hit rate before building it?
- What is the failure mode of a semantic cache and how would you measure it?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-021">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> You run long inference jobs through a queue. Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, and what your workers must do as a result.</summary>

A queue decouples producers from workers and absorbs bursts. Its delivery guarantee
decides what the worker code must tolerate.

- **At-most-once.** The message is acknowledged before processing. A crash loses the
  job. Acceptable only for work that can be dropped.
- **At-least-once.** The message is acknowledged after processing; if the worker dies or
  the visibility timeout expires first, it is redelivered. Nothing is lost, but a job
  can run twice, including when the first run actually finished and only the
  acknowledgement was lost. This is what almost every system provides.
- **Exactly-once.** Not achievable as pure delivery over an unreliable network. What
  systems offer is exactly-once *effect*: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or
  transactional processing.

So workers must be **idempotent**:

- Give every job an idempotency key. Before doing work, or atomically with writing the
  result, check whether that key is already complete.
- Write results with an upsert keyed by the job id, never an append.
- For side effects outside your store (sending a message, charging a customer), pass the
  idempotency key downstream or record intent and completion transactionally.

Other things to design:

- *Visibility timeout* longer than the worst-case processing time, or a heartbeat that
  extends it. A GPU job that outlives its timeout is run twice concurrently.
- *Retries with backoff* and a **dead-letter queue** after N attempts, so that a poison
  message does not block the queue forever.
- *Ordering* only where needed, per key, since global ordering costs throughput.
- *Backlog age* as the main metric for autoscaling and alerting.

A log such as Kafka differs from a task queue: consumers track an offset in an ordered,
replayable partition, which suits event pipelines; per-message acknowledgement and
retries suit job processing.

**Follow-ups**

- Where exactly does the duplicate come from when a worker finishes just as its timeout expires?
- How do you make "send the user an email with the result" idempotent?

</details>


### Data validation and pipeline quality <span class="demand">9% of postings</span> {#data-quality}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.data-quality.0"> Define a data contract and place validation at ingestion, before training and at serving
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.data-quality.1"> Write checks for schema, nulls, ranges, categories, volume and freshness
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="mlops.data-quality.2"> Trace a silent upstream change to the model's inputs and plan the backfill

<details class="qa" id="mlops-026">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> What is a data contract, and where do you put data validation in an ML pipeline?</summary>

A data contract is an explicit agreement between the producer of a dataset and its
consumers: the schema (names, types, nullability), the semantics and units of each
field, allowed values and ranges, freshness and completeness expectations, the owner,
and how changes are announced and versioned. Its purpose is to turn a silent upstream
change into a failed check on the producer's side.

Validation belongs at three points, each catching a different failure:

1. **At ingestion**, on each batch or stream window. Schema and types, primary-key
   uniqueness, null rates, value ranges and categories, row counts against expectation,
   and freshness. Bad data is quarantined before it spreads to derived tables.
2. **Before training**, on the assembled training set. Label rate and label
   distribution, feature distributions against the previous snapshot, duplicates, and
   leakage between splits. Fail the pipeline; do not train.
3. **At serving**, on each request. Type and range checks, missing features, and
   unknown categories, with a defined fallback and a counter. Then compare serving
   distributions with training.

Kinds of check, from cheap to subtle: schema; volume and freshness; per-column
statistics (nulls, min, max, distinct count, quantiles); cross-column rules (end after
start); referential integrity; distribution comparison with a reference.

Practical points: thresholds learned from history with tolerance bands work better than
hand-set constants; classify checks into blocking and warning, or people learn to ignore
them; every check needs an owner who is paged; and the expectations should be stored
with the dataset version so that training and serving validate against the same
definition.

**Follow-ups**

- Which checks block the pipeline and which only warn, and how do you decide?
- How do you validate a free-text or image column?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-027">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">coding</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Write a small validation function for a pandas DataFrame that a training pipeline can run as a gate. What would you add for production?</summary>

```python
import pandas as pd

def validate(df: pd.DataFrame, spec: dict, min_rows: int = 1) -> list[str]:
    """spec: {col: {"dtype": str, "max_null": float, "min": x, "max": x,
    "values": set, "unique": bool}}. Returns a list of problems; empty means pass."""
    errs = []
    if len(df) < min_rows:
        errs.append(f"only {len(df)} rows, expected at least {min_rows}")
    for col, rule in spec.items():
        if col not in df.columns:
            errs.append(f"{col}: missing column")
            continue
        s = df[col]
        if "dtype" in rule and str(s.dtype) != rule["dtype"]:
            errs.append(f"{col}: dtype {s.dtype}, expected {rule['dtype']}")
        null_rate = s.isna().mean()
        if null_rate > rule.get("max_null", 0.0):
            errs.append(f"{col}: null rate {null_rate:.3f}")
        v = s.dropna()
        if "min" in rule and (v < rule["min"]).any():
            errs.append(f"{col}: values below {rule['min']}")
        if "max" in rule and (v > rule["max"]).any():
            errs.append(f"{col}: values above {rule['max']}")
        if "values" in rule:
            extra = set(v.unique()) - rule["values"]
            if extra:
                errs.append(f"{col}: unexpected values {sorted(extra)[:5]}")
        if rule.get("unique") and v.duplicated().any():
            errs.append(f"{col}: duplicate values")
    return errs
```

The pipeline calls it and fails when the list is non-empty, logging every problem, not
only the first.

What production adds:

- **Distribution checks** against the previous snapshot (quantiles, category shares,
  label rate), with tolerance bands learned from history.
- **Freshness and volume** relative to the same weekday, not a constant.
- **Cross-column and cross-table rules**: timestamps in order, foreign keys present,
  no overlap between train and test keys.
- **Severity levels** and quarantine of bad partitions instead of all-or-nothing.
- **Scale**: the same rules compiled to SQL or Spark for data that does not fit in
  memory. Libraries such as Great Expectations, pandera or TFDV provide this; the logic
  is what an interviewer wants to see.
- The spec versioned next to the dataset, and reused for serving-time checks.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you check that no user appears in both the training and the test split?
- Where do the thresholds come from, and who updates them?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="mlops-028">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> A model has been slowly getting worse for two weeks. You find that an upstream team changed how a field is populated, so one feature is now null for a third of rows. What do you do now and what do you change afterwards?</summary>

**Contain.** Decide quickly between rolling the upstream change back, patching the
feature computation to read the new source, or serving without the feature. If the model
degrades gracefully with the feature missing, a temporary imputation matching what
training saw may be enough; if the null is being mapped to a default such as zero that
means something else to the model, fix that first, since a wrong value is worse than a
missing one.

**Assess the damage.** Three places are affected:

1. *Serving* for two weeks: quantify the metric loss and who was affected.
2. *Logged features*: any training data built from this period contains the broken
   feature. Mark the range.
3. *Models retrained during the period*: they learned from corrupted data and may now
   depend on the null pattern. Check whether an automatic retrain was promoted.

**Repair the data.** Backfill the feature for the affected dates from the corrected
source if it can be recomputed as of each event's time; otherwise exclude the range or
keep it with an explicit missing indicator. Rebuild downstream tables and retrain from
clean data. Backfills must be idempotent and must not overwrite point-in-time
correctness.

**Prevent.**

- A null-rate and distribution check on this feature at ingestion and at serving, with
  an alert that pages its owner. Two weeks of unnoticed decay means input monitoring was
  missing or ignored.
- A data contract with the upstream team, with schema and semantics tests in their
  deployment pipeline and a registered list of consumers.
- A data-validation gate before every retrain.
- A feature-importance-weighted view of input health, so that the features that matter
  get the strict thresholds.

In the retrospective, the question is not who changed the field but why the system
allowed a silent change to reach a model.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you have detected this on day one?
- The backfilled values differ slightly from what was served. Which do you train on?

</details>
